---
title: Designing view transitions
description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.
nav_title: View transitions
---

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

part.text:
Done. View transitions are wired up following Next.js 16's React `<ViewTransition>` model (no config flag needed). `next build` passes typecheck and both routes render/stream correctly.

**What changed:**
- `types/react-canary.d.ts` — references `react/canary` so `ViewTransition`/`addTransitionType` are typed.
- `app/ProductGrid.tsx` — each thumbnail wrapped in `<ViewTransition name={`product-${slug}`} share="morph" default="none">`; links tagged `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}`.
- `app/product/[slug]/page.tsx` — hero wrapped in the same morph `name`; Suspense fallback wrapped `exit="slide-down"` and content `enter="slide-up"`; whole page root is a directional `<ViewTransition>` keyed by `nav-forward`/`nav-back` (`default: 'none'`); back link tagged `nav-back`.
- `app/page.tsx` — same directional root wrapper + Suspense reveal wrappers.
- `app/globals.css` — `.morph` (blur-softened), `.slide-down`/`.slide-up` (skeleton→content), `.nav-forward`/`.nav-back` (directional slides), `::view-transition { pointer-events: none }`, and a `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` block that zeroes all view-transition durations **and** disables the skeleton shimmer.

**How the requirements map:**
1. *Image morph* — shared `view-transition-name: product-${slug}` on both thumbnail and hero → browser morphs size/position; `default="none"` keeps it from animating on unrelated transitions.
2. *Directional slides* — `transitionTypes` on Links → `addTransitionType` runs inside the navigation transition; each page's root `<ViewTransition>` maps `nav-forward`/`nav-back` to the slide classes (forward = left, back = right). The directional wrapper is the page root (required: enter/exit only fire when no DOM node sits above the `<ViewTransition>`).
3. *Suspense reveal* — fallback `exit="slide-down"`, content `enter="slide-up"` with asymmetric timing; plays on the detail page's 100ms `ProductDetails` resolve.
4. *Reduced motion* — the media query neutralizes every `::view-transition-*` animation plus the pulse shimmer.

Note: browser back/forward (popstate) intentionally doesn't carry a transition type, so it won't directional-slide (a React/View-Transitions limitation); the shared-element morph still applies there. The `package.json`/`tsconfig.json` edits shown in `git diff` were auto-applied by Next.js during build, not by me.
